opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say my confidence comes from a few places, and honestly it's more cautious than some people might expect.

First, there's the empirical side. Over the past few years we've seen that models can already do parts of their own improvement loop. They generate training data, critique their own outputs, write code that gets executed and verified, and search over reasoning paths with feedback from verifiers. In domains where you can check the answer, like math, programming, and certain games, this works remarkably well. AlphaGo Zero and its successors showed this years ago: a system playing against itself, with a clear reward signal, can go far beyond human-level play without human data. So the basic principle that a system can bootstrap itself is not science fiction. We've seen it.

Second, there's a structural argument. Human-generated data is finite, and we're getting close to using most of the high-quality text available. If we want continued progress, the system has to be able to produce new knowledge, or at least new useful training signal, on its own. So self-improvement isn't just an interesting idea. It's almost a necessity if scaling is going to continue.

Third, and this is something I care about as a researcher, we're starting to understand why these things work. Looking at training dynamics, how representations form, how a model discovers structure in data, gives me more confidence than black-box results alone. If you understand the mechanism, you can design better loops rather than just hoping they work.

That said, I'm careful to separate what we know from what we hope. Self-improvement works best when there's a reliable verifier. In open-ended areas, like research taste, judging what's an important problem, or creative work, the feedback signal is much noisier, and a system can easily drift or reward-hack instead of genuinely getting better. So I'd say I'm confident in the direction, but the hard and interesting problem is how to extend self-improvement beyond domains with clean rewards. That's where a lot of the real research is right now.

r001.rationale: The response says self-improvement works well in verifiable domains and describes existing capabilities, but it does not state that each incremental stage of progress delivers practical application value.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think my confidence comes less from any single result and more from a pattern I kept running into over the years.

When I was working on game-playing agents, the most striking thing wasn't that the systems got strong. It was where the strength came from. Once you give a model a reliable signal about whether it did well, and you let it generate its own experience and learn from that, you stop being bottlenecked by what humans can write down. The system discovers things we didn't teach it, and sometimes things we didn't know. That shift, from imitating human data to producing and verifying its own, is the core of what people now call self-improvement.

The second reason is that for a lot of the problems we actually care about, verification is much cheaper than generation. Math, code, reasoning, planning, these are domains where you can check an answer far more easily than you can produce it. Whenever that asymmetry exists, you can set up a loop: the model proposes, something checks, and the feedback goes back into training. That loop doesn't require more human-labeled data. It requires compute and a good verifier. Compute keeps scaling, and we're getting better at building verifiers, so the trend line points one way.

The third thing is that we're already seeing the early version of this work in practice. Models trained with reinforcement learning on reasoning tasks improve on problems that weren't in their training distribution. Models can write test cases, critique their own outputs, and act as judges for other models. None of these is a fully closed loop yet, but each piece has gone from a research idea to something that actually moves benchmarks.

Now, I want to be honest about what I'm not confident in. The hard part is the verifier. When the reward is noisy or gameable, self-improvement becomes self-deception. The model gets very good at satisfying the signal instead of solving the problem. And in open-ended domains, say scientific discovery or long-horizon planning, we still don't have good ways to tell the model what "better" means. So I'd put it this way: I'm confident the direction is right, because the underlying logic is sound and the ingredients are getting cheaper. Whether it's two years or ten before it works broadly depends on how fast we solve the evaluation problem, not the learning problem.

r001.rationale: The response says early self-improvement techniques have moved benchmarks, but it does not state that every incremental stage of progress delivers practical application value.

astra-6.text:
What gives me confidence is that we’ve already seen a limited form of it work when a system can reliably evaluate its own results. Think about a game: you can try different strategies, play against yourself, and get a clear signal about whether you’re improving. You don’t need a human to label every move.

The interesting question is how far we can extend that process. In coding, for example, a model can propose a solution, run tests, observe failures, and try again. That creates a feedback loop where generating more attempts can actually lead to better results, provided the tests capture what you care about.

But I would distinguish that from a model simply generating more text and training on it. That alone doesn’t guarantee improvement; it can reinforce mistakes. You need a source of feedback that can tell you something you didn’t already know.

So my confidence is in that mechanism: exploration, feedback, and learning. The challenge is making the feedback reliable as we move from problems with clear answers to more open-ended tasks. That’s why I see self-improvement as a promising research direction, rather than something we should assume will happen automatically.

r001.rationale: The response gives game and coding examples of feedback-driven improvement, but does not state that every incremental stage of progress delivers practical application value.

sol-6.1.text:
What gives me confidence is that we already have settings where an AI can generate experience, evaluate the results, and improve from that feedback. Self-play is a good example: you don’t need a human to label every move. The rules give you a signal, and the system can discover strategies through repeated interaction.

For language models, the question is where we can build a similarly reliable loop. Coding and mathematics are promising because you can often check an answer with tests or a verifier. The model can propose a solution, see what fails, and try again. That creates an opportunity to learn beyond simply imitating existing examples.

But generating more text is not automatically self-improvement. If the feedback is weak, the model can reinforce its own mistakes or learn to exploit the evaluator. So my confidence is conditional: when we have reliable verification, enough exploration, and a way to turn successful experience into learning, I think this is a very powerful direction.

r001.rationale: The response describes promising self-improvement loops and conditional potential, but does not state that each incremental stage of progress delivers practical application value.
